title: How do you read line charts and spot the trends that matter in a case?
description: How to read line charts in case interviews: trends, turning points, growth rates and the dual-axis trap, with a worked example of two companies' sales.
hook: Read a line chart by checking the axes first, then looking for the turning point (when the trend changed), the gap between lines (and whether it is widening), and the growth rate, rather than reading out each year's value. Line charts show change over time, and they are where candidates most often describe instead of think.
body:
What to look for

  • Direction: rising, falling or flat.
  • Turning points: when did the trend change, and what happened then?
  • Gaps: the distance between two lines, and whether it is widening or closing.
  • Growth rates: a steeper line means faster growth in absolute terms, but not necessarily in percentage terms.

How to read one in 30 seconds

  1. Read the axes. Units, time period, whether the vertical axis starts at zero, and whether there are two vertical axes.
  2. Name the overall trend in one sentence.
  3. Find the turning point or the widening gap. That is usually the insight.
  4. Put a number on it: a growth rate, a gap in dollars or a change in share.
  5. Ask what happened at that moment, and say what you would investigate.

A worked example

A chart shows the client's sales and its main rival's over five years ($M):

YearClientRival
1100100
2112110
3125122
4126138
5127155

Both grew at 10% to 12% a year until year 3. Then the client's line flattens, growing under 1% a year, while the rival's keeps climbing at about 13% a year. By year 5 the rival is $28M ahead.

Strong: "The client kept pace until year 3, then stalled while the rival kept growing at around 13% a year. The gap is now $28M and widening. Something changed in year 3: a new product, a price move or a new channel. That's what I'd investigate first."
Weak: "In year 1 both were at 100. In year 2 the client was at 112 and the rival at 110. In year 3..."

The strong answer finds the turning point, quantifies the gap and turns it into a question. The weak one reads the table aloud.

Levels versus rates

A line chart in dollars shows absolute change, which can mislead when the lines start at different sizes. Company A grows from $100M to $120M; company B from $10M to $15M. On the chart, A's line rises much more steeply: $20M against $5M. In percentage terms, A grew 20% and B grew 50%.

Neither view is wrong; they answer different questions. If the question is who is gaining momentum, use percentages. If it is who is adding the most revenue, use dollars. Say which one you mean. For growth rates over several years, compound growth and CAGR shows the quick method.

If the vertical axis is on a log scale, equal slopes mean equal percentage growth, which makes rates easy to compare but absolute gaps hard to judge.

Seasonality

Monthly and quarterly figures often follow a seasonal pattern. If a retailer peaks every December, a fall from December to January is normal, not a crisis. To see the underlying trend, compare each month with the same month last year, or use a rolling twelve-month total.

Common traps

  • Reading every value aloud instead of finding the turning point.
  • A vertical axis that does not start at zero. A line rising from 96 to 104 on an axis running from 95 to 105 looks dramatic, but it is an 8% rise.
  • Dual axes. When two lines use different scales on the left and right, their crossing point means nothing, and whoever drew the chart can make them track closely just by adjusting the scales. Read each line against its own axis and compare growth rates instead.
  • Mixing percentages and absolute values on the same chart without noticing.

Practice

1. A retailer's monthly sales fell from $12M in December to $8M in January. Last January they were $7M. Is the business in trouble?

Show the answer

Probably not. The December to January fall looks like seasonality. Year on year, January sales are up from $7M to $8M, about +14%. "Compared with last January, sales are up 14%, so the drop looks seasonal. I'd check the same comparison for the last few months to confirm the trend."

2. A chart's vertical axis runs from 95 to 105. Weekly orders, in thousands, rise from 96 to 104 over the period. The line climbs almost the full height of the chart. How big is the change?

Show the answer

An increase of 8 on a base of 96 is about 8%. The truncated axis makes it look as if orders almost doubled. Always check where the axis starts before describing the size of a change.

Where to practise next

For the general routine for any exhibit, read how to read a chart in a case. Line charts are common in market entry cases, where market growth decides a lot. Practise in the chart reading drill and the graph library.
